title: Tennis Says: Same Game, Same Prize Money!
summary:
Imagine winning a tennis tournament and finding out the prize money is different just because you're a girl or a boy. That's been happening in some big tennis events for years. But now, that's changing.

The Women's Tennis Association (WTA) announced that starting next year, men and women will get equal prize money at all combined 1,000 events. These are the biggest tournaments outside the four Grand Slams. Some places like Indian Wells, Miami, Madrid, and Beijing already did this. But now the Italian Open, Canadian Open, and Cincinnati Open will too.

The WTA was formed in 1973 to fight for women's tennis. Valerie Camillo, the WTA chair, called this a "major milestone." American player Jessica Pegula said the changes give players more power to plan their own seasons.

Players will also have fewer required tournaments, so they can rest more. It's a big win for fairness in sports!
why_it_matters: If you play a sport at school, this shows that speaking up when something isn't fair can change the rules — and it could mean more chances and support for girls' teams in the future.

background_read: The Women's Tennis Association (the WTA — a group that runs women's professional tennis around the world) was created in 1973 by players led by the American champion Billie Jean King, who fought for women to be treated fairly.
That same year, the U.S. Open became the first of tennis's four biggest tournaments to give men and women the same prize money, but Wimbledon (the famous British tournament) only did that much later.
Jessica Pegula is an American tennis star, and Valerie Camillo is the WTA chair — the leader who speaks for the whole group.

WHY: To make tennis fair for women players and give them more power to plan their seasons, with fewer required tournaments so they can rest

perspectives.perspective: Players and fans who say it's about time
perspectives.description: They believe women train and play just as hard as men, so winning the same tournament should mean earning the same money.

perspectives.perspective: People who say the change is too slow
perspectives.description: They point out that it only starts next year and only covers some tournaments, so the four Grand Slams and smaller events are still not all equal.

perspectives.perspective: Sports experts watching the bigger pattern
perspectives.description: They say tennis has been slowly moving toward equal pay since the 1970s, and this is the next step in a long trend rather than a sudden surprise.
